opus-5.5.text:
I think system prompting is genuinely one of the most underrated levers we have, but also one of the most misunderstood. When we worked on Llama 2, a lot of the effort on the chat side went into making the model actually respect the system prompt over many turns. Early on, you'd give the model an instruction like "always answer as if you were a pirate" or "respond only in French," and after three or four turns it would just forget. That's why we came up with things like Ghost Attention, a fairly simple trick in the fine-tuning data so the model learns to keep attending to that initial instruction throughout the dialogue. It sounds minor, but for orchestrating agents it's fundamental: if your agent can't hold onto its role and constraints over a long trajectory, nothing else you build on top is reliable.

Now, for agents specifically, I'd say system prompts are necessary but not sufficient. You can describe a role, the tools available, the format of the outputs, and that gets you surprisingly far, especially with strong models. Multi-agent setups where one model plays the planner, another the executor, another the critic, all differentiated mostly by prompting, actually work, and that tells you how much instruction following has improved.

But I'm a bit skeptical that prompting alone is the long-term answer. Prompts are brittle. Small wording changes give you different behaviors, and as tasks get longer, with dozens or hundreds of steps, errors compound. What really moves the needle is when the model has been trained, through RLHF or more recently RL on actual agentic trajectories with tool use and feedback from the environment, to follow instructions and recover from its own mistakes. Then the system prompt becomes more of a specification and less of a crutch.

So my view: system prompting is the interface, and it's a good one because it's natural language and anyone can use it. But the capability underneath, robust instruction following, planning, self-correction, has to come from training. The best results come when the two are co-designed, where you train the model knowing how people will prompt it, and you prompt it knowing what it was trained to do.

r001.rationale: The response says prompting alone is necessary but not sufficient, describes prompts as brittle, and argues that robust orchestration also depends on training.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest moving agent orchestration into latent space.

r003.rationale: It says multi-agent setups differentiated mostly by prompting already work and that prompting gets surprisingly far, indicating impressive existing results.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think system prompting is, honestly, a bit of a hack that we've all come to rely on, and it's worth being clear-eyed about why it works and where it breaks.

When we did Llama 2 and then Llama 3, a big part of the post-training effort was instruction following, and system prompts were really the first lever we had to steer behavior at inference time without touching the weights. You tell the model "you are a helpful assistant, you have access to these tools, here's the format," and the model, because it's been trained on enough of that distribution, more or less complies. That's powerful because it's cheap. Anyone can orchestrate agents by writing text. No gradient steps, no data pipeline.

But the limitations show up pretty fast once you go from a single chat turn to a multi-step agent. A few things I've seen. First, instruction following degrades with context length and with the number of constraints. You give the model twenty rules in the system prompt, and by step fifteen of a trajectory it's honoring maybe twelve of them. That's not a prompting problem, it's a training problem. The model was never really optimized for long-horizon adherence, it was optimized for short, single-turn preference data. Second, there's a fragility to it. Reorder two sentences, change a verb, and you get different behavior. We saw this a lot in evals. If your orchestration depends on brittle phrasing, you're building on sand.

And the third point, which I think is the deeper one, is that system prompting treats the model as a static thing you're configuring from the outside. The agent doesn't learn from the environment. It doesn't get better at the task it's actually doing. You're essentially doing few-shot or zero-shot adaptation forever.

So my view is that prompting is the right starting point and a terrible end state. The direction I care about is moving the orchestration logic into training. Instead of telling the model how to use tools in a prompt, you train it on trajectories where it uses tools, gets feedback, and learns what works. That's what we were pushing toward with agentic post-training, and it's really what reinforcement learning on environments is about. The system prompt becomes a thin layer, maybe just specifying the task, and the competence lives in the weights.

There's also an interesting middle ground where the prompt is itself something the system learns or searches over, so you're not relying on a human to hand-craft it. But I'd still frame that as a transitional technique.

The last thing I'd say is that instruction following as a capability is underrated as a research target precisely because everyone treats it as solved. It's not. Robust, long-horizon, compositional instruction following is close to the core of what makes an agent reliable, and if we got that genuinely right, a lot of today's orchestration scaffolding would just disappear.

r001.rationale: The response calls system prompting a “terrible end state,” describes instruction-following failures in long agent trajectories, and argues orchestration logic should move into training.

r002.rationale: It proposes moving orchestration into training and model weights, but does not say it needs to move into latent space.

r003.rationale: It says prompting is cheap and powerful, but does not clearly claim that prompt-based orchestration already achieves impressive results.

astra-6.text:
I think system prompting is useful, but it’s only as reliable as the model’s ability to follow instructions. You can describe an agent’s role, give it tools, tell it when to delegate—but writing those instructions doesn’t guarantee that the behavior will hold over a long sequence of actions.

So I’d distinguish between what you ask the model to do and what your software actually enforces. The model can make decisions where you need flexibility, while the surrounding code handles permissions, validates actions, and defines clear stopping conditions.

The interesting question is how much of that orchestration the model can learn. If you find yourself adding another instruction for every failure, that’s a signal that prompting alone isn’t solving the underlying problem. You need to evaluate complete tasks and improve the model’s ability to recover from mistakes, not just its ability to produce a convincing next response.

r001.rationale: The response says prompting alone does not solve orchestration and contrasts it with software enforcement, judging prompting and instruction following alone as insufficient.

r002.rationale: It asks how much orchestration the model can learn, but does not suggest moving orchestration into latent space.

r003.rationale: It calls system prompting useful, but does not say that prompting and instruction following already achieve impressive results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think instruction following is really what makes agents possible. You can have a very capable model, but if you can’t reliably tell it what to do, it’s difficult to build a system around it. With a system prompt, you can define a role, give it access to tools, and specify when it should use them.

But I would distinguish describing the behavior from actually getting that behavior reliably. You can write, “Make a plan, execute it, check your work,” and the model may do that on a simple example. The question is whether it keeps following those instructions over a long trajectory, when a tool fails or something unexpected happens.

So I see prompting as a very useful interface for experimenting with agent orchestration. You can quickly try different workflows. But the quality of the agent still depends on the underlying model and how well it has been trained to follow instructions, use tools, and recover from mistakes. A more elaborate system prompt doesn’t automatically give you a more capable agent.

r001.rationale: The response says prompting alone does not ensure reliable behavior or a more capable agent, and that capability also depends on the underlying model and its training.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest moving agent orchestration into latent space.

r003.rationale: It describes prompting as useful for experimentation and says it may work on simple examples, but does not say this approach already achieves impressive results.
